title: Diagnostic and Interventional Pediatric Cardiac Catheterisation
subject: ss-paediatric-cardiology

steps.say: In the catheter laboratory we measure output without any flow probe, using oxygen consumption and the oxygen gap across the circulation instead.
steps.tx: Output is calculated by the **Fick principle**. Cardiac output equals oxygen consumption (VO2 in mL per min) divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference (arterial oxygen content minus venous oxygen content), so a wide oxygen gap with normal consumption indicates a low output state requiring urgent support.

vis.caption: Severe pulmonary venous hypertension and marked vascular congestion on chest radiography. Illustration: StewardMD original.
vis.alt: Chest radiograph showing severe pulmonary vascular congestion.

steps.say: Comparing saturations from four sampling sites tells you how much blood is short circuiting through a septal defect, expressed as a single ratio.
steps.tx: Shunt size is expressed as a **shunt calculation formula (Qp to Qs ratio)**. Pulmonary flow (Qp) divided by systemic flow (Qs) equals systemic arterial saturation minus mixed venous saturation, divided by pulmonary venous saturation minus pulmonary arterial saturation, with a ratio above 1.5 generally considered haemodynamically significant and worth closing.

rows: Mixed blood actually reaching the body
Oxygenated return and mixed pulmonary flow

steps.say: A sudden jump in oxygen saturation as the catheter advances from one chamber to the next pinpoints exactly where the hole sits.
steps.tx: Location is identified by the **oximetric step up**. A saturation increase of **7-8% or more** between the right atrium and right ventricle confirms a left to right ventricular shunt, while a **9-10%** rise from the caval veins to the right atrium confirms an atrial level shunt.

left.title: Atrial Level Shunt
points: Step up of 9 to 10 percent from SVC or IVC to right atrium
Oxygenated left atrial blood enters at the atrial level
Seen in atrial septal defects and partial anomalous drainage

right.title: Ventricular Level Shunt
points: Step up of 7 to 8 percent from right atrium to right ventricle
Oxygenated blood enters at the ventricular level
Seen in ventricular septal defects and aortopulmonary window

steps.say: The smallest patients face a specific vascular risk from arterial access, so every infant case ends with a careful limb perfusion check.
steps.tx: Access carries a risk of **femoral artery thrombosis (vascular access complications)**. Femoral artery thrombosis occurs in up to **3-5%** of infants undergoing arterial catheterisation, presenting with a pale pulseless limb that is treated with systemic heparinization (blood thinning) or recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to dissolve the clot.

rows: Single anterior wall stick with micropuncture set
Fewer passes and less intimal injury
Activated clotting time monitoring during the case
Shortest length that reaches the target
Preserves distal perfusion in tiny vessels

steps.say: Children are far more sensitive to radiation than adults, so the laboratory follows strict dose sparing habits on every case.
steps.tx: Exposure is limited by **pulsed fluoroscopy**. Pediatric catheterization radiation mitigation uses pulsed fluoroscopy at **3-7.5 pulses/second** under **radiation dose reduction (ALARA)**, low dose detector settings, and strict collimation (narrowing the beam to the region of interest), with stored last image hold replacing repeat screening runs.

nodes.label: Collimate tightly to the cardiac silhouette before any pedal press
Use pulsed fluoroscopy at 3-7.5 pulses/second with low dose mode
Review last image hold instead of re screening the same view
Record dose area product and audit outliers monthly

steps.say: Device closure of the ductus looks tempting, but three specific situations make it unsafe and each has a clear physiological reason.
steps.tx: Closure has defined **transcatheter PDA closure contraindications**. Ductal occlusion using Amplatzer duct occluders is contraindicated in neonates with active sepsis, severe pulmonary hypertension with right to left shunt, or duct dependent systemic lesions, because closing the ductus in these settings removes the only pathway sustaining life.

left.title: When Closure Is Unsafe
points: Active sepsis with bacteraemia risks seeding the device with infection
Severe pulmonary hypertension with right to left shunt needs pop off
Duct dependent systemic circulation collapses without ductal flow

right.title: When Closure Is Appropriate
points: Haemodynamically significant ductus with left heart volume overload
Child beyond the prostaglandin dependent window and infection free
Pulmonary pressures low enough to tolerate loss of the shunt

steps.say: For a narrowed aorta the catheter laboratory now offers a definitive fix, and the choice between balloon and stent depends mainly on the size of the child.
steps.tx: Obstruction is treated by **balloon coarctation angioplasty**. Balloon angioplasty is the intervention of choice for native coarctation in older children and for recoarctation after surgery, while covered stenting (a fabric lined scaffold) is preferred in adolescents above **35 kg** whose near adult aortic size accepts a stent safely.

rows: Avoids surgery and grows with the child
Scarred reoperative field makes redo surgery hazardous
Adult sized aorta holds the scaffold with wall protection

steps.say: The final numbers from the catheter tell you how stiff and overloaded the left ventricle is, and there are clear cut offs to remember.
steps.tx: Filling pressures are judged by **left ventricular end diastolic pressure**. Normal resting left ventricular end diastolic pressure in children is **6-12 mmHg**, while values above **15-18 mmHg** indicate elevated left sided filling pressures from volume overload, diastolic dysfunction, or obstructive left heart disease.
